reviews.response:
Verdict: ACCEPT for the completion theorem and the  $8\times12$  obstruction, with one necessary qualification to the dual-matroid formulation.The qualification is:If  $B$  is not saturable from the full set  $T$ , there are no exterior-feasible  $q$ -sets. If  $B$  is saturable from  $T$ , those  $q$ -sets are exactly the bases of the dual transversal matroid.This rank condition is automatic whenever the refined assignment graph is feasible. It should nevertheless appear in a statement that also covers infeasible instances.The coordinate example is correct, including both good completions and the obstruction outside the specified normal form. I give explicit matching certificates below. I have not run your code or inspected a repository.1. Precise matching and cost conventionsFor a self-contained theorem, make the following conventions explicit: $M$  has vertex support exactly  $P$ . Thus every vertex of  $Q$  is unmatched by  $M$ .A relay’s charged cost is
$$\ell(R)=\sum_{e\in E(R)\cap M}w(e).$$
For a full physical matching  $N$ , the objective is
$$\Phi(N)=
\sum_{t\in T}\ \sum_{e\in E(C_t(N))\cap M}w(e),
\tag{1}$$
where  $C_t(N)$  is the terminal alternating path containing  $t$  in the multigraph  $M\cup N$ . Paths starting in  $W$ , and components contained entirely in  $P$ , contribute zero.Replace “unused actual edges may be doubled” by “unused  $M$ -edges may be doubled in  $M\cup N$ .” The constructed  $N$  itself is an ordinary matching.These conventions agree with the supplied unit-cost paths: each displayed length-three relay contains one  $M$ -edge, so a  $T$ -relay has fee one. Charging every grid edge would give a different objective.Under (1), assigning weight zero to  $z-i$  is correct even when the chosen  $W$ -relay traverses positively weighted  $M$ -edges.2. The normal-form correspondence is validWrite  $r=|I|$ . Because  $M$  matches every core internally,  $P$  is balanced. Balance of  $V$  therefore gives
$$|T|+|W|=|B|+r,$$
so the two sides of  $K$  have equal cardinality.Lifting an assignment to a physical matchingLet  $J$  be a perfect matching of  $K$ . For each edge of  $J$ :For  $t-i$ , select a minimum-cost  $T$ -relay to  $h_i$ .For  $z-i$ , select any witnessing  $W$ -relay to  $h_i$ .For an edge to  $b\in B$ , select the corresponding actual direct grid edge.These selected paths are vertex-disjoint:Their  $Q$ -endpoints are distinct because  $J$  is a matching.Each centre is used once.The interior of the path to  $h_i$  lies in  $P_i$ , and distinct cores are disjoint.There is also no problem with the unused part of  $P$ . Every interior vertex of an  $M$ -alternating relay appears together with its  $M$ -mate: the path starts and ends with non- $M$  edges, so its interior is partitioned into whole  $M$ -edges.Let  $R$  be the union of the selected paths, including the direct terminal edges. Then
$$N=M\mathbin{\triangle}E(R)
\tag{2}$$
is a perfect matching of  $V$ . The path flips cover all terminal endpoints and all relay interiors; the retained  $M$ -edges cover the remaining vertices of  $P$ .Thus the one-relay-per-core restriction supplies exactly the disjointness needed for simultaneous physical realization.Contracting a physical normal-form matchingConversely, let  $N$  be a full physical matching in the stated normal form. Contract each terminal alternating path of  $M\cup N$ :A  $T$ -to- $h_i$  relay produces  $t-i$ .A  $W$ -to- $h_i$  relay produces  $z-i$ .A direct terminal-to- $B$  component produces its direct assignment edge.Every terminal endpoint appears once, so the contracted edges form a perfect matching of  $K$ . Components entirely in  $P$  disappear under this contraction.The precise cost statement is
$$\operatorname{cost}_K(J)\le \Phi(N)$$
for an arbitrary physical representative of  $J$ , with equality attained by choosing minimum-cost  $T$ -relays. Consequently,
$$\boxed{
U_{\rm dir}
=
\min_{\substack{J\text{ perfect}\\\text{matching of }K}}
\operatorname{cost}_K(J)
=
\min_{\substack{N\text{ physical}\\\text{in normal form}}}\Phi(N).
}
\tag{3}$$
Thus arbitrary relay choices need not preserve assignment cost, but the minimum cost within each contracted assignment is exactly its weight in  $K$ .Hall certificates and unrestricted scopeA complete Hall test can be written on the right side:
$$|N_K(D\cup J)|\ge |D|+|J|
\qquad
(D\subseteq B,\ J\subseteq I).
\tag{4}$$
Failure yields a certificate for normal-form infeasibility.Here “involving  $B$  and centres” should mean that the certificate ranges over their union. A particular violating set may lie entirely in  $B$ , entirely in  $I$ , or contain both.For the unrestricted optimum,
$$f^*\le U_{\rm dir}.$$
Infeasibility of  $K$  establishes absence of a normal-form completion. Equality with the unrestricted optimum requires a lower bound valid for arbitrary physical matchings. The board example below supplies such a lower bound.3. The Hall inequalities are exact; the dual-base statement needs the rank provisoNow forbid  $W$ -to- $B$  edges. Every  $W$ -vertex must be matched to a distinct centre, so precisely
$$q=r-|W|=|T|-|B|$$
centres must receive  $T$ -relays.For  $D\subseteq B$ , write
$$N(D)=N_T(D),
\qquad
s(D)=|N(D)|-|D|.$$
Fix  $A\subseteq T$  with  $|A|=q$ . Since  $|T\setminus A|=|B|$ , Hall’s theorem gives
$$\begin{aligned}
B\text{ is saturable from }T\setminus A
&\iff |N(D)\setminus A|\ge |D|
   &&\text{for every }D\subseteq B\\
&\iff |A\cap N(D)|\le s(D)
   &&\text{for every }D\subseteq B.
\end{aligned}
\tag{5}$$
This equivalence is correct without any preliminary feasibility assumption.Exact matroid formulationLet  $\mathcal M_B$  be the transversal matroid on ground set  $T$ , whose independent sets are subsets matchable into  $B$ . This is the standard transversal-matroid construction. nvlpubs.nist.govPut
$$\nu=r_{\mathcal M_B}(T).$$
If  $\nu<|B|$ , no deletion of vertices from  $T$  can make  $B$  saturable. Hence the feasible  $q$ -set family is empty. But  $\mathcal M_B^*$  still has bases, all of cardinality
$$|T|-\nu>|T|-|B|=q.$$
Therefore the feasible family cannot equal the entire dual-base family in this case.If  $\nu=|B|$ , then
$$\begin{aligned}
A\text{ is exterior-feasible}
&\iff T\setminus A\text{ is a basis of }\mathcal M_B\\
&\iff A\text{ is a basis of }\mathcal M_B^*.
\end{aligned}
\tag{6}$$
An unconditional formulation, retaining the cardinality restriction explicitly, is
$$\boxed{
\{\text{exterior-feasible }q\text{-sets}\}
=
\mathcal B(\mathcal M_B^*)\cap\binom{T}{q}.
}
\tag{7}$$
The intersection is empty in the rank-deficient case.Rank interpretationThe matching rank has the Hall-deficiency formula
$$r_{\mathcal M_B}(X)
=
\min_{D\subseteq B}
\bigl(|B|-|D|+|X\cap N(D)|\bigr).
\tag{8}$$
Assuming full exterior rank,  $r_{\mathcal M_B}(T)=|B|$ , duality yields
$$\begin{aligned}
r_{\mathcal M_B^*}(A)
&=|A|+r_{\mathcal M_B}(T\setminus A)-|B|\\
&=\min_{D\subseteq B}
\bigl(|A\setminus N(D)|+s(D)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\tag{9}$$
Since
$$|A\setminus N(D)|+s(D)
=
|A|+s(D)-|A\cap N(D)|,$$
equation (9) proves, for arbitrary  $A\subseteq T$ ,
$$A\text{ is independent in }\mathcal M_B^*
\iff
|A\cap N(D)|\le s(D)\quad\forall D\subseteq B.
\tag{10}$$
For  $|A|=q$ , independence is equivalent to being a dual basis.Your slack consequences follow exactly:A zero-slack neighbourhood permits no deletion from that neighbourhood.A slack-one neighbourhood permits at most one deletion from it.Two individually exposable ports can form a dependent pair in the dual matroid.One further scope distinction belongs in the statement: a dual basis certifies exterior feasibility. Full completion also requires a perfect matching from  $A\sqcup W$  to  $I$  in the centre-reachability graph. The original assignment graph  $K$  enforces both requirements simultaneously.4. The cores are pairwise nonadjacent. The unique white  $Q$ -vertex with more than one  $P$ -neighbour is

which is adjacent to  $(3,5)\in P_0$  and  $(5,5)\in P_2$ . Every other white  $Q$ -vertex has at most one  $P$ -neighbour. All four neighbours of each centre belong to its ring, so there are no direct  $T$ -centre edges.Name the four ports
$$a=(4,9),\qquad a'=(3,8),\qquad
c=(5,8),\qquad c'=(4,7).$$
The supplied matching orientation gives the following alternating relays:RelayActual path $M$ -edge traversedCharged fee $A$  $(4,9)\to(3,9)\to(2,9)\to(2,10)$  $(3,9)(2,9)$  $1$  $A'$  $(3,8)\to(3,9)\to(2,9)\to(2,10)$  $(3,9)(2,9)$  $1$  $C$  $(5,8)\to(5,7)\to(6,7)\to(6,6)$  $(5,7)(6,7)$  $1$  $C'$  $(4,7)\to(5,7)\to(6,7)\to(6,6)$  $(5,7)(6,7)$  $1$  $H$  $(4,5)\to(3,5)\to(3,4)\to(2,4)$  $(3,5)(3,4)$  $0$ The last path is the required  $W$ -relay to  $h_0$ . Its fee is zero despite traversing a unit-weight  $M$ -edge.Since no  $T$ -centre edge is direct, every  $T$ -relay contains an  $M$ -edge. Thus the four displayed  $T$ -relay costs are also their respective minimum costs.5. Each resulting 33-edge matching saturates all of  $B$  using precisely the complement of the indicated centre-source pair.Combining these exterior matchings with respectively

(A',C,H)$$
and retaining the unused  $M$ -edges gives two full physical matchings.For a direct cardinality check, each has: $33$  direct exterior edges; $6$  non- $M$  edges from the three relay flips; $9$  retained  $M$ -edges.That is  $48$  disjoint matching edges covering all  $96$  vertices. reviews.response:
Referee reportACCEPT WITH REQUIRED DOCUMENTATIONOverall mathematical verdict: The q-root source-budget theorem and the shared-slack potential theorem are correct under the stated hypotheses. The fixed  $12\times18$  all- $K$  obstruction also has a sound lower-bound argument. I find no mathematical contradiction in their central inequalities or in the proposed  $K+1$  lower bound.There is, however, an important distinction between proving the lower bound and proving the claimed exact attainment. The coordinate certificate containing the direct exterior matching is referenced but not included in the supplied material. Consequently, the exact equality in (5) is not independently established by the two notes alone.I give the detailed reasoning below.1. q-root exact source-budget attainment theoremProof correctLet  $I$  denote the set of  $r$  centres. Write  $W$  for the  $r-q$  HH sources.The dummy-root assignment construction is correct. Introduce  $q$  additional left vertices, each adjacent to every  $i\in I$  with cost  $\rho_i$ . The original HH sources have their zero-cost edges to reachable centres.A perfect assignment then has cost exactly
$$\sum_{i\text{ unmatched by the HH assignment}}\rho_i.$$
Consequently, (2) is indeed an ordinary minimum-weight assignment problem.1.1 The lower boundConsider an arbitrary full physical auxiliary matching  $N$ .Let  $k$  be the number of TH paths ending at centres.There are  $r-k$  HH paths ending at centres. These produce a partial matching in  $\Gamma$ , with  $r-k$  distinct matched centres.The remaining  $k-q$  HH sources end in exterior  $B$ .The partial HH-centre matching can be extended to one saturating  $W$ . The relevant point is that an augmenting path beginning at an unmatched left vertex and ending at an unmatched right vertex preserves every previously matched right vertex.Thus the  $q$  centres left unmatched by the extended matching belong to the original  $k$  TH centres.Call this subset  $J$ . Since every TH-centre path is a local relay under the separated-core assumptions,
$$f(N)
\geq \sum_{i\text{ TH centre}}\rho_i
\geq \sum_{i\in J}\rho_i
\geq \Lambda_q.$$
This proves the nontrivial lower bound.In particular, the argument does not incorrectly allocate an independent copy of an HH source to each centre. It uses one globally injective assignment.1.2 The strict-positivity equivalenceThe proof of (4) is also correct.Suppose
$$f^*=\Lambda_q.$$
Because the board is finite, a minimizing physical matching exists.If  $k>q$ , the first inequality above is strict relative to the selected  $q$  centres:
$$\sum_{i\text{ TH centre}}\rho_i
>
\sum_{i\in J}\rho_i
\geq\Lambda_q,$$
since every  $\rho_i>0$ .Therefore  $k=q$ .It follows that:Every HH source serves a centre.Every centre TH path is among the  $q$  selected TH paths.All remaining TH paths end in  $B$ .Equality of the total expense with  $\Lambda_q$  forces the remaining TH paths to have zero expense.Since every actual edge has strictly positive weight, a zero-expense TH path cannot contain an actual edge. It must therefore be a direct  $Q$ -to- $Q$  edge.The minimizing physical matching consequently belongs to the  $U_c$  class. Hence
$$U_c\leq f^*=\Lambda_q.$$
Together with the general lower bound,
$$\Lambda_q\leq f^*\leq U_c,$$
this gives  $U_c=\Lambda_q$ .Conversely, if  $U_c=\Lambda_q$ , its attaining assignment constructs a full physical auxiliary matching, so
$$\Lambda_q\leq f^*\leq U_c=\Lambda_q.$$
Thus (4) follows.1.3 Nonnegative weightsThe weaker sufficient statement is correctly distinguished:
$$U_c=\Lambda_q\quad\Longrightarrow\quad f^*=\Lambda_q.$$
Strict positivity is needed for the reverse implication, not for this implication.With zero-weight actual edges, a non-direct exterior TH path can have zero expense. The argument forcing all exterior TH paths to be direct then fails.This is an appropriate distinction, not a gap.1.4 One clarification worth addingThe extension argument should explicitly say that the partial HH-centre matching has size  $r-k$ , and that an augmenting path preserves its already matched right vertices.The existing text essentially says this, but spelling out the invariant makes the key subset assertion completely transparent.No theorem correction is required.2. Shared-slack potential theoremProof correctThis is the strongest part of the new argument. In particular, the shared HH budget is accounted for correctly even when the Hall regions overlap or are nested.2.1 Exact accounting identityThe definitions give
$$\sum_{t\in T}\phi_T(t)
-
\sum_{b\in B}\phi_B(b)
=S.$$
Since  $\pi$  is a bijection from  $T\sqcup W$  to  $B\sqcup C$ , and  $\phi_B$  vanishes on centres,
$$\sum_{t\in T}\phi_B(\pi(t))
+
\sum_{w\in W}\phi_B(\pi(w))
=
\sum_{b\in B}\phi_B(b).$$
Subtracting,
$$\begin{aligned}
A-L
&=\sum_{t\in T}
  \bigl(\phi_T(t)-\phi_B(\pi(t))\bigr)\\
&=S+\sum_{w\in W}\phi_B(\pi(w)).
\end{aligned}$$
This proves the equality in (1).There is no multiplicity error: an HH endpoint contributes its potential once, regardless of how many regions contain it.2.2 Counting the HH exterior endpointsExactly  $r-k$  centres receive HH paths.Since there are  $r-q$  HH sources, the remaining number is
$$(r-q)-(r-k)=k-q.$$
Those endpoints must lie in  $B$ .By definition,
$$0\leq \phi_B(b)\leq\mu.$$
Therefore
$$S\leq A-L\leq S+(k-q)\mu.$$
The use of the black maximum  $\mu$ , rather than a maximum over both colour classes, is correct.2.3 Positive compensation forces non-direct pathsFor a direct exterior edge  $t-b$ , if  $b\in D_j$ , then
$$t\in N_T(D_j)=F_j.$$
Consequently,
$$\phi_T(t)\geq\phi_B(b).$$
Thus a positive compensation,
$$\phi_B(\pi(t))-\phi_T(t)>0,$$
is impossible on a direct edge.It is also impossible when  $\pi(t)$  is a centre, because its black potential is zero.Therefore every positively compensating path ends in exterior  $B$  and is non-direct.Each such path has compensation at most  $\mu$ . Hence
$$z\mu\geq L.$$
From the accounting identity,
$$L=A-S-\sum_{w\in W}\phi_B(\pi(w)),$$
and the shared HH endpoint bound gives
$$L\geq A-S-(k-q)\mu.$$
Therefore
$$z\geq
\max\left\{0,
\left\lceil
\frac{A-S-(k-q)\mu}{\mu}
\right\rceil\right\}.$$
The ceiling and maximum operations are correct, including when the right-hand numerator is negative.2.4 Replacing  $A$  by  $R$ For every  $t$  whose endpoint is a centre,
$$\phi_B(\pi(t))=0.$$
Its contribution to  $A$  is exactly  $\phi_T(t)$ .All other contributions to  $A$  are nonnegative. Therefore
$$A\geq R.$$
This proves the second inequality in (2).2.5 The physical cost lower boundThe  $k$  TH-centre paths are necessarily non-direct because centres have no direct selected neighbours.The  $z$  positively compensating exterior paths are also non-direct.They are distinct components of the physical matching and cannot share actual matching edges.Each such path contains at least one actual edge. When all actual weights are at least one, their combined cost is at least  $k+z$ .Thus (3) follows.Importantly, the proof does not charge actual edges on HH paths. This remains true even if their actual-edge weights are very large.2.6 Tight-set specializationFor  $s_j=0$ , the identity reduces to the tight-region accounting.For a single unit-weight tight region, with  $q=1$ , it gives
$$z\geq \max\{0,\lceil A-k+1\rceil\}.$$
The stated specialization is consistent.No correction to the shared-slack theorem is required.3. Fixed  $12\times18$  all- $K$  obstructionLower-bound argument correctI checked the essential coordinate and cost logic separately.3.1 Board and matching countsThe board has
$$12\cdot18=216$$
vertices, with 108 of each colour.Each  $5\times5$  core has 24 vertices after removing its centre.The three cores therefore contain 72 vertices, matched by 36 actual edges per? More precisely, each core contributes 12 matching edges, giving
$$|P|=72,\qquad |M|=36.$$
The remaining 144 vertices form  $Q$ , with 72 vertices of each colour.The stated terminal counts
$$|T|=71,\quad |W|=1,\quad |B|=69,\quad |C|=3$$
are consistent.The three cores are pairwise nonadjacent.3.2 The HH relayThe displayed path
$$(6,7),(5,7),(5,6),(5,5),(4,5),(3,5)$$
has the correct structure.Its two actual matching edges are
$$(5,7)-(5,6),
\qquad
(5,5)-(4,5).$$
These belong to the core-0 matching pattern.The other two path edges connect the endpoints to the centre and HH source using auxiliary incidences.The HH cost is zero, notwithstanding the actual weights of its two matching edges.This distinction is essential and is used correctly.3.3 The two cheap centre relaysThe first cheap actual edge is
$$(5,15)-(4,15),$$
and the second is
$$(9,11)-(9,10).$$
They belong to different cores.The associated paths are
$$(6,15),(5,15),(4,15),(3,15)$$
and
$$(9,12),(9,11),(9,10),(9,9).$$
The endpoint colours, core membership, and actual matching incidences are consistent.The assertion that the black endpoint has a unique white  $Q$ -neighbour is correct:For  $(5,15)$ , the other white neighbours lie in the first core, and the only white  $Q$ -neighbour is  $(6,15)$ .For  $(9,11)$ , the other white neighbours lie in the third core, and the only white  $Q$ -neighbour is  $(9,12)$ .The white endpoint in each case is adjacent to its corresponding centre.Since every other actual edge has weight  $K$ , a TH centre relay costing less than  $K$  must use one of these two cheap actual edges. The uniqueness observations then force precisely the displayed relays.This establishes the claimed cheap-only classification.3.4 The 17/18 Hall regionLet
$$R=\bigl(\{6\}\times[13,17]\bigr)
\cup
\bigl([7,11]\times[12,17]\bigr).$$
The black vertices in  $R$  number 17 and the white vertices number 18.The boundary check is important:The left exterior neighbours of black vertices on  $x=6$  belong to core 1.The lower exterior neighbours at  $y=11$  belong to core 2.The upper and right exterior neighbours lie outside the board.All remaining white neighbours lie in  $R$ .Thus no additional selected white neighbour occurs outside the proposed region.All 18 white vertices in  $R$  are selected, and every one is adjacent to a black vertex of  $D$ .Consequently,
$$N_T(D)=F,\qquad |D|=17,\qquad |F|=18.$$
Both cheap entrances lie in  $F$ .Deleting them leaves only 16 white neighbours for 17 black vertices.
